children: By Sara Randazzo
"You are not Atticus Finch."

That's the message Silicon Valley lawyer Ivan Gaviria delivered to nine of Gunderson Dettmer's newest partners during a recent boot camp on how to successfully win business and stand out against AI and competitors, stressing that "you have to accept that you are in the business of sales."

As AI tools become more sophisticated and companies decide they can do more legal work themselves, law firms are increasingly betting that lawyers will distinguish themselves through something artificial intelligence can't easily replicate: relationships.

Being a successful partner, Gaviria told his junior colleagues, is like being that favorite guide on a safari or outdoor excursion. The goal is to become “someone who they want to hang out with at the fireplace afterwards, but who they also trust to keep them safe on the mountain.”

With around 400 lawyers, Gunderson Dettmer Stough Villeneuve Franklin & Hachigian focuses exclusively on representing venture-backed technology and life sciences companies and investors, including the lead investors this year in a $65 billion financing for Anthropic. People skills may be even more key to its business than at the typical law firm, because its lawyers must woo startup founders who have often never worked with an attorney before.
As Gunderson partner Ryan Purcell told the trainees, he aims to be Tom Hagen, the consigliere to the Corleone family in the “Godfather.”

Trainings like the one I sat in on at Gunderson are one part of answering a question plaguing many law firms. As AI tools become more sophisticated, and companies decide they can do more legal work themselves, what are law firms bringing to the table?

It’s not just a theoretical concern. Law firm partners tell me clients now send them documents they’ve drafted themselves with AI and ask them to simply review them. Companies like AT&T have created entire AI-powered teams of in-house lawyers that do research and legal work that would have been done by law firms.

Gaviria told the assembled Gunderson partners that it used to be easier, when billing rates were lower, to have junior lawyers sit in on pitches and learn through an apprenticeship model. Now, they have to find time on the law firm’s dime — like letting the nine trainees and half a dozen senior partners dedicate the better part of that September day to an event that no client would pay for.
A TRUSTED GUIDE

The boot camp exuded Silicon Valley vibes. Lawyers — clad in the local uniform of company-branded hooded windbreakers, jeans and fancy sneakers — dropped F bombs, alongside talk of wild happy hours. A beloved cornhole set sat propped in one corner of the room.

At the same time, the partners’ hard-charging work ethos came through. Gunderson partner Trevor Knapp, for instance, reminded his colleagues that “there’s no replacement for the extra hour of work at 6 in the morning or on the weekends.”

Over the course of the day, the trainees, all in their first five years in the partnership, heard tips from firm veterans on how to win and keep clients, workshopped their own personal brands, role-played tricky client scenarios and learned the economics of law-firm billing. The firm is repeating the training soon for new partners from its East Coast offices.
The junior partners in attendance were hesitant to speak with me, lest they come off to clients as being inexperienced.

Even as the boot camp emphasized the human relationships that set lawyers apart from AI, it also showcased ways technology could strengthen those connections. One AI tool the firm is developing will send a nudge to a partner when a new executive joins one of their clients, along with a template for an email introduction.

Gunderson isn't alone in doubling down on people skills. Consultant John Childers said he started getting calls six years ago from firms asking him to help set new partners on the path to generating business rather than acting as glorified senior associates doing other people’s work. Firms are willing to invest in having him run a six-month program, he said, because the payoff can be immense if it leads to partners having more confidence to bring in work.

“A big part of it is getting new partners to think of themselves differently,” Childers, who has worked with Gunderson, said. “For years you're super reactive, with people giving you what needs to be done. Suddenly you turn the corner and it's time to be proactive, and for some that's daunting.”

Back in Silicon Valley, Gaviria, whose clients have included DoorDash and leather goods company Cuyana, emphasized that being good at business development is not innate and that it’s a skill that took him years to perfect.

The seasoned partners imparted tips big and small to keep clients close, including taking the word "busy" out of your vocabulary when talking to clients and knowing when to pick up the phone rather than emailing.

They also talked about how to spot the super connectors who will send you business. Gaviria said as a young partner he tracked every referral for a few years and realized some people he consistently took to baseball games and lunch never sent him any work, versus someone he met once at a board meeting who sent him five leads. “You have to ruthlessly manage your time," he said.

The Gunderson partners shared how they fight getting sidelined when their startup clients hire an in-house lawyer for the first time. In one such instance, Gaviria said he helped the new general counsel look good during a strategy meeting by texting him answers in real time as the company lawyer got stuck on questions. The result? "He was a loyal customer for like six more years after that," he said.
